title: Files, directories, links & archives
about: The directory tree and paths, inodes, hard and symbolic links, copying, moving and removing, mounting and disk space, and archives with tar and gzip.

questions.title: One tree for everything
questions.text: How does Linux present its storage devices to the user?

options.t: As a single hierarchical tree starting at `/`, where other file systems are attached at directories.
options.why: There are no drive letters; a second disk simply appears under some directory.

options.t: As separate trees named `C:`, `D:`, and so on.
As a flat list of files with no directories.
As one tree per user, each rooted in the home directory.
options.why: There is one system-wide tree; homes are branches of it.

questions.title: Absolute or relative
questions.text: Classify each path.

items.why: Starts with `/`, so it is resolved from the root regardless of where you are.
It begins at the root; the `..` inside does not change that.
No leading slash: resolved from the current directory.
Starts from the parent of the current directory.
`.` is the current directory; the path is still relative.

questions.title: Special directory names
questions.text: Match each notation with its meaning.

pairs.r: The current directory
The parent directory
Your home directory
The home directory of user luke
pairs.why: The shell looks the user up.

pairs.r: The previous directory
pairs.why: Jumps back to where you were.

extras.r: The root of the file system

questions.title: Root directory and parent
questions.text: What does `cd ..` do when you are already in `/`?

options.t: You stay in `/`, because the root's parent is itself.
options.why: There is nothing above the root.

options.t: It moves you to your home directory.

questions.title: cd without arguments
questions.text: Which command always takes you to your home directory?

options.why: Bash reads `$HOME` when no directory is given.
That stays in the current directory.

questions.title: Ways to print the current directory
questions.text: Which of these print the current working directory?

options.why: The shell keeps the path in this variable.
It lists the *contents*, not the directory's own path.
It changes directory and prints nothing.

questions.title: Hidden files
questions.text: Which statement about hidden files is correct?

options.t: A file is "hidden" simply because its name starts with a dot; `ls -a` shows it.
options.why: There is no separate hidden attribute in Unix.

options.t: They have a special permission bit called `h`.
They cannot be opened by normal users.
options.why: Hidden files are readable like any other.

options.t: They are stored in a secret area of the disk.

questions.title: ls options
questions.text: Match each option with its effect.

pairs.r: Include hidden files, also `.` and `..`
Include hidden files, but not `.` and `..`
Long format with permissions, owner, size and date
pairs.why: One line of detail per entry.

pairs.r: Recurse into sub-directories
Show the inode number of each entry

extras.why: That is `-S`, not any of these.

questions.title: First character of ls -l
questions.text: In the output of `ls -l`, what does the first character of the mode field, `d` in `drwxr-xr-x`, tell you?

options.why: `-` would be a regular file and `l` a symbolic link.
Deletability depends on the parent directory's permissions.

options.t: The entry is a hidden file.
options.why: Hidden files are recognised by their name, not by this flag.

questions.title: Create nested directories
questions.text: To create `a/b/c` in one go, even when `a` and `b` do not exist yet: `mkdir {{0}} a/b/c`
questions.note: Without `-p`, `mkdir a/b/c` fails if `a/b` is missing.

wrong.why: `-r` is not an option of `mkdir`; `-r` is for recursion in `cp`, `rm` and `ls -R`.

questions.title: Removing a directory
questions.text: Which statement about `rmdir` is correct?

options.t: It removes a directory only if it is empty.
options.why: To delete a directory with contents use `rm -r`.

options.t: It removes a directory and everything inside it.

options.why: It does not filter by name.

options.t: It moves the directory to a trash folder.
options.why: Unix has no global trash in the shell.

questions.title: rm on a directory
questions.text: What does `rm somedir` (no options) do when `somedir` is a directory?

options.t: It refuses and prints `Is a directory`.
options.why: You need `-r` (or `rmdir` for an empty one).

options.t: It deletes the directory if it is empty.
options.why: That is what `rmdir` does, not plain `rm`.

options.t: It deletes the directory and its contents.

questions.title: What an inode stores
questions.text: Select the information that is stored in an inode.

options.why: Stored in the inode, not in the directory.

options.t: The size and the time stamps.
The location of the file's data blocks on disk.
options.why: The inode points to where the contents are.
Names live in directory entries, which point to inodes.

questions.title: What a directory is
questions.text: What is a directory, internally?

options.t: A special file containing a list of names, each paired with the inode number of the file it names.
options.why: Names belong to directories, not to inodes.

options.t: A folder that physically contains the file data.
options.why: Data lives in blocks referenced by inodes.

options.t: A copy of every file below it.
options.why: Directories hold only the name→inode mapping.

questions.title: Why a rename is cheap
questions.text: Why is `mv file1 file2` inside one file system practically instant, even for a huge file?

options.t: Only the directory entry (the name) changes; the inode and the data blocks stay exactly where they are.
Because the file is moved to the trash.
Because the data is always small in Linux.
options.why: Size is irrelevant to a rename.

questions.title: Hard link meaning
questions.text: What is a hard link created with `ln f hard`?

options.t: A second directory entry (name) that points to the same inode as `f`.
options.why: Both names are equal; neither is "the original".

options.t: A small file that stores the path `f`.
A copy of `f` with its own inode and data blocks.
options.why: A copy would be independent; a hard link is not.

options.t: A reference that dies when `f` is deleted.
options.why: Hard links survive the removal of any one name.

questions.title: Hard or symbolic link
questions.text: Which kind of link has the described property?

items.t: Shares the inode of the original
items.why: Both names point to the very same inode number.

items.t: Still works after the other name is deleted
items.why: The data exists until the last name is removed.
The kernel forbids hard links to directories to avoid loops.

items.t: Can point to a file on another file system
items.why: It stores only a path, so it can cross file systems.

items.t: Becomes a broken link if the target is removed
items.why: The path then points to nothing.

items.t: Has its own inode, shown with type `l` in `ls -l`
items.why: It is a tiny file containing a path.

questions.title: Link count
questions.text: `ls -l` shows a number right after the mode field, for example `-rw-r--r-- 2 user group`. What is that `2`?

options.t: The number of directory entries (hard links) that point to that inode.
The number of users who can read the file.
The size of the file in blocks.
The number of times the file was opened.

questions.title: Delete one name
questions.text: A file `f` has a hard link `g`. After `rm f`, what is true?

options.t: The contents remain available through `g`, and the link count drops from 2 to 1.
options.why: The file disappears only when the count reaches 0 and nothing has it open.
That is how a *symbolic* link behaves.
`rm` removes only the name you give.
Nothing is moved; `g` always pointed to the same data.

questions.title: Broken symlink
questions.text: You create `ln -s f soft`, then run `rm f`. What happens with `cat soft`?

options.t: It fails with "No such file or directory", because the link still exists but its target does not.
It prints the old contents of `f`.
options.why: The data belonged to `f`; a symlink stores only its name.
The link is a separate directory entry.

questions.title: Create a symbolic link
questions.text: To create a symbolic link named `short` that points to `/usr/share/dict/words`: `ln {{0}} /usr/share/dict/words short`
questions.note: The argument order is like `cp`: target first, link name second. Without `-s` you get a hard link.

wrong.why: Not the option to make a symbolic link in `ln`.

questions.title: ln argument order
questions.text: In `ln -s target linkname`, which argument is the existing file?

options.why: The first is what you link *to*; the second is the new name you create.
That is the name that will be created.

options.t: Neither, `ln` needs a third argument with the directory.

questions.title: Directory link counts
questions.text: An empty directory shows a link count of 2 in `ls -ld`. What happens to that count when you create a sub-directory inside it?

options.t: It becomes 3, because each sub-directory's `..` entry points back to the parent.
options.why: The count is 2 plus the number of sub-directories.
The `..` entries add to the parent's count.

options.t: It increases for every file, not for directories.
options.why: Files do not add links to their parent.

questions.title: Symbolic link facts
questions.text: Select the true statements about symbolic links.

options.t: They can point to a file that does not exist (a dangling link).
options.why: The path is not checked at creation time.

options.t: They share the inode of their target.
They keep the data alive after the target is deleted.
options.why: The data is owned by the target's inode.

questions.title: Permissions of a symlink
questions.text: Why does `ls -l` show `lrwxrwxrwx` for every symbolic link?

options.t: The permissions of the link itself are not used; access is decided by the permissions of the file it points to.
options.why: The kernel follows the link first.

options.t: Because every symbolic link is executable.
Because only root can create them.
Because the target's permissions are copied into the link.

questions.title: Basic file commands
questions.text: Match each command with what it does.

pairs.r: Makes a copy of `a` named `b`
pairs.why: A new file with its own inode.

pairs.r: Renames `a` to `b`, or moves it
pairs.why: Same inode when on the same file system.

pairs.r: Removes the name `a`
pairs.why: The data goes when no names remain.

pairs.r: Creates `a` if absent, or updates its timestamp
pairs.why: Often used to make an empty file.

pairs.r: Creates the directory `d`

questions.title: cp options
questions.text: Select the correct statements about options of `cp`.

options.why: Without it `cp` refuses to copy a directory.
A safety net against accidental overwrites.

options.t: `-u` copies only when the source is newer or the destination is missing.
`-a` preserves attributes and copies recursively, keeping symbolic links as links.

options.why: `-l` makes hard links instead of copies; `-v` lists.

questions.title: Copying a symlink
questions.text: `cp soft copy` where `soft` is a symbolic link to a regular file. What is `copy`?

options.t: A regular file with the target's content, because `cp` follows the link by default.
options.why: Use `-P` or `-a` to copy the link itself.

options.t: A symbolic link to the same target.

options.why: It contains the data of the target.

questions.title: mv a directory
questions.text: `mv dirA dirB` when `dirB` already exists and is a directory. What happens?

options.why: If `dirB` did not exist it would be a rename.
Non-empty directories are not replaced by `mv`.

options.t: The contents of `dirA` are merged into `dirB`.
The command fails because the target exists.
options.why: It works and nests the directory.

questions.title: rm -i
questions.text: Which option makes `rm` ask for confirmation before each removal?

options.why: Interactive mode; handy when working as root.
Forces removal without asking, ignoring non-existent files.
Recursion, it does not ask by itself.

questions.title: The dangerous rm
questions.text: Which command is the most dangerous one if a variable turns out empty, as in `rm -rf "$DIR"/*` with `DIR` unset?

options.t: It expands to `rm -rf /*`, attempting to delete everything the user can.
options.why: Always check variables before recursive deletion.
It asks for every file, which gives you a chance to stop.

questions.title: touch on a missing file
questions.text: What does `touch newfile` do when `newfile` does not exist?

options.t: It creates an empty file with that name.

questions.title: Set a date
questions.text: To create `old` with the modification date set to 2 January 2020 (date only): `touch {{0}} "2020-01-02" old`

wrong.why: `-t` also sets a time, but needs a different stamp format `[[CC]YY]MMDDhhmm[.ss]`, not this string.

questions.title: Temporary files
questions.text: What does `mktemp` provide compared with choosing a name like `/tmp/out`?

options.t: A unique, unpredictable file name, created safely, so two runs do not collide.
options.why: It prints the name of the new file.

options.t: A file that is deleted automatically when the script ends.

options.why: `/tmp` may be RAM-backed on some systems, but `mktemp` does not guarantee that.
It creates an empty file or directory.

questions.title: Wildcard deletion
questions.text: In a directory you run `rm *.txt`. Which files does the shell pass to `rm`?

options.t: Every file whose name ends in `.txt`, expanded before `rm` starts.
options.why: Globbing is done by the shell, not by `rm`.

options.t: Only one file at a time.
options.why: All matches are passed as arguments.

options.t: The literal text `*.txt`, which `rm` then interprets.
options.why: Only when no file matches and `nullglob` is off.

questions.title: What mounting does
questions.text: What does `mount /dev/sdb1 /mnt/usb` do?

options.t: It attaches the file system on that device to the directory `/mnt/usb`, so its files appear there.
options.why: The directory is the mount point.

questions.title: Unmount
questions.text: Which command detaches a mounted file system?

options.why: Note the spelling: there is no `n` after `u`.
It would try to remove a directory.

questions.title: Disk space tools
questions.text: Match each command with its output.

pairs.r: Free and used space of each mounted file system in human-readable units
Total size used by a directory tree, human-readable
pairs.why: Looks at the files below a path.

pairs.r: The list of mounted file systems
Inode metadata of a file (size, links, times, permissions)
An indented picture of a directory tree

questions.title: df versus du
questions.text: What is the main difference between `df` and `du`?

options.t: `df` reports space per file system (free and used), while `du` adds up the space used by the files of a path.
options.why: One looks from the disk, the other from the files.

options.t: `df` works only for directories, `du` only for files.
options.why: Both work at different scopes; this split is wrong.

options.t: `du` shows free space, `df` shows file sizes.
They are the same program with two names.

questions.title: Human-readable
questions.text: What does the `-h` option do in `df -h` and `du -h`?

options.t: Prints sizes in units like K, M and G instead of raw blocks.

questions.title: Depth of du
questions.text: Which command shows the space used by each sub-directory of the current directory, but not deeper?

options.why: Limits the recursion to one level below the starting point.

questions.title: Full disk vs. du
questions.text: `df` says a file system is 100% full, yet `du` of its top directory adds up to much less. Which explanation is plausible?

options.t: A deleted file is still held open by a running process, so its space is not freed yet.
options.why: `du` no longer sees the name, `df` still counts the blocks.
That would make it higher, not lower.

options.t: `df` measures in bits and `du` in bytes.

questions.title: Archive versus compression
questions.text: What is the difference between tar and gzip?

options.t: `tar` bundles several files and directories into one archive file; `gzip` compresses one file or stream.
options.why: They are often combined to get `.tar.gz` or `.tgz`.

questions.title: tar options
questions.text: Match each tar option with its meaning.

pairs.r: Create an archive
Extract files from an archive
List the contents of an archive
Filter through gzip
pairs.why: Compresses on creation, decompresses on extraction.

pairs.r: The next argument is the archive file name
pairs.why: Without it tar uses a default device.

pairs.r: Verbose: show files as they are processed

extras.why: `tar` never removes the originals on its own.

questions.title: Create a compressed archive
questions.text: To create a gzip-compressed archive `backup.tgz` containing the directory `docs`: `tar {{0}} backup.tgz docs`
questions.note: The option letters may be combined; `f` has to be last of the group since it takes the next argument.

wrong.why: `x` extracts; it would fail because `backup.tgz` does not exist yet.

questions.title: Extract a compressed archive
questions.text: To extract `backup.tgz` into the current directory: `tar {{0}} backup.tgz`
questions.note: Add `-C dir` to extract somewhere else.

wrong.why: `c` would try to create (and overwrite) the archive.

questions.title: List before extracting
questions.text: Before extracting an archive from an untrusted source, you want to see which files it contains. Which command does that?

options.why: Would try to create an archive.
It shows compression statistics, not the files inside the tar.

questions.title: gzip removes the original
questions.text: What does `gzip notes.txt` do by default?

options.t: It compresses the file in place without renaming it.

questions.title: gunzip
questions.text: How do you decompress `notes.txt.gz`?

options.why: `tar` extracts archives, not single gzip files.

questions.title: File extensions
questions.text: Match each extension with what you expect.

pairs.r: An uncompressed tar archive
A file compressed with gzip
A tar archive compressed with gzip
A file compressed with the old `compress` command

questions.title: Backup workflow
questions.text: Put these steps of making and verifying a compressed backup in order.

items.t: Create the archive: `tar czf b.tgz docs`
items.why: Nothing else can happen before the file exists.
Check that the files you expect are inside.
Only worth copying after the check.

items.t: Extract a test copy in a temporary directory
items.why: The real test of a backup is restoring it.

questions.title: Order of tar arguments
questions.text: You meant to archive `notes.txt` into `notes.tgz` but typed `tar czf notes.txt notes.tgz`. What is the damage?
questions.note: With a directory in that position tar would fail with "Is a directory" instead; with a plain file, the original data is silently lost.

options.t: The first name after `f` is the archive to write, so `notes.txt` is overwritten by a gzip archive, which contains the file `notes.tgz`.
options.why: The archive name goes right after `f`; the files to add follow.

options.t: None: tar always sorts its arguments so that the archive comes last.
options.why: It does not guess; the position after `f` decides.

options.t: tar refuses and prints a help message.
options.why: It performs exactly what you wrote.

questions.title: Count entries
questions.text: In an empty directory `d` you run `touch a b; mkdir c; ls -l d | wc -l` from its parent. What number is printed?

options.why: `ls -l` prints a "total" line plus one line per entry (a, b, c).
That forgets the header line `total N`.

questions.title: Copy into itself
questions.text: What does `cp -r dir dir/copy` (copying a directory into itself) do in GNU `cp`?

options.t: It refuses with an error like "cannot copy a directory into itself".
It creates `dir/copy` with all the contents of `dir`.
options.why: That is what a copy to a *different* place would do.

questions.title: Link count after creating links
questions.text: A file has a link count of 1. You run `ln f h` and `ln -s f s`. What is the link count of `f` now?

options.why: The hard link `h` adds one; the symbolic link `s` is a separate file and does not count.
A symbolic link does not increase the target's count.
The hard link added a name.
Counts never go to zero while names exist.

questions.title: Overwritten on mv
questions.text: `mv a b` where `b` already exists as a regular file (and no `-i` or alias). What happens?

options.why: That is why many people alias `mv` to `mv -i`.

options.t: The command asks for confirmation by default.

questions.title: Current dir in a script
questions.text: Immediately after `mkdir -p a/b/c && cd a/b/c && cd ../..`, where are you relative to the starting directory?
